title: A Pedigree for the Induction Head

body:
The claim that *induction heads* carry most of in-context learning in transformers has been in print for four years. In 2022 Olsson, Elhage, and twenty-odd colleagues at Anthropic laid out six lines of evidence for it and were careful to flag the central one — the connection to ICL in large models — as preliminary and indirect. The evidence was correlational: induction heads appear mid-training, in-context learning appears mid-training, the two coincide to the point of showing a small bump in the loss curve, and attention patterns in the trained model do look like what the circuit predicts. What was missing was a counterfactual. Which training examples, specifically, are responsible for the formation of that head? Remove them and does the head fail to form? Add more and does it form earlier?

In July 2026 an ICML oral by Chen, Luo, and Pan supplies that counterfactual. They take Pythia's reproducible training trajectory, pick a specific interpretable unit — an induction head — rank every training sample by its influence on the strength of that head, remove the top-ranked slice, and watch the head fail to form on schedule. They then run the mirror experiment and watch it form earlier. The samples that top the ranking are not what the induction-head story predicted. They are LaTeX, HTML, and XML.

## Why this matters now

Three results sit under this one. In 2022 Olsson et al. proposed the induction head as the central ICL circuit, with the ICL link flagged "preliminary and indirect". In 2023 Grosse, Bae, Anil, Elhage and co-authors at Anthropic showed that *influence functions* can be scaled to a 52-billion-parameter model via an eigenvalue-corrected Kronecker factorisation of the Hessian (EK-FAC), making it tractable to ask "which training example moves this test behaviour?" at frontier scale. The same year Biderman and colleagues released Pythia: sixteen checkpointed models trained on fully public data in a fully specified order, which is the one artefact that lets you re-run a training trajectory and intervene on it. In between, Park, Georgiev, Ilyas, Leclerc, and Madry introduced TRAK, a sampling-based attributor that uses random projections of the empirical NTK to attribute predictions in a few thousand training-model runs. The toolkit was complete; the move Chen et al. make is to point the attributor not at a model prediction but at the formation of a named circuit. That move is what *mechanistic data attribution* names.

## What influence functions actually estimate

Fix a training set $\{z_1, \dots, z_n\}$, a loss $L(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell(z_i,\theta)$, and an empirical risk minimiser $\hat\theta = \arg\min L$. Upweight training sample $z_j$ by $\varepsilon$ and let $\hat\theta_{j,\varepsilon}$ be the perturbed minimiser. By an implicit-function argument around $\hat\theta$, for any smooth scalar functional $f$ of parameters,

$$\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} f(\hat\theta_{j,\varepsilon})\right|_{\varepsilon=0} \;=\; -\nabla_\theta f(\hat\theta)^\top H^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell(z_j,\hat\theta),$$

where $H = \nabla^2_\theta L(\hat\theta)$ is the empirical Hessian. Setting $\varepsilon = -1/n$ gives a first-order approximation to the leave-one-out counterfactual. The quantity $I_j(f) = -\nabla_\theta f(\hat\theta)^\top H^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell(z_j,\hat\theta)$ is called the influence of $z_j$ on $f$. Classical uses pin $f$ to a test loss on a held-out example. Nothing in the derivation requires that choice. $f$ can be any differentiable scalar on parameter space.

The methodological hinge is a careful choice of $f$. Pick $f$ = the mean *head-matching score* of a specific attention head on a prefix-matching probe set, i.e. the mean attention mass this head places on the previous occurrence of the current token in sequences of the form $A B \dots A \to B$. That scalar is zero when the head is random, approaches one when the head is a clean induction head, and is differentiable through the softmax. Any training sample $z_j$ whose influence on this $f$ is large is a sample whose presence pushes the model's parameters toward the subspace in which this specific head computes the induction algorithm. The ranking is causal in the influence-function sense: it is a first-order estimate of how much the head's score would drop if that sample were removed from training.

## Making it tractable

Computing $H^{-1} v$ at the scale of a billion-parameter model is the whole game. EK-FAC, due to Martens and Grosse (2015) and sharpened by George et al. (2018), replaces $H$ by a block-diagonal Kronecker factored approximation layer by layer, then corrects the eigenvalues of each block against empirical Fisher statistics. The resulting approximation to $H^{-1}$ is cheap to apply and, Grosse et al. 2023 report, correlates well with the gold-standard PBRF estimator while running orders of magnitude faster. For an attributor pass over Pythia-scale training data this is the difference between infeasible and routine, and newer libraries (Bergson, Peng et al. 2026) make the gradient-store side of the pipeline distributed and on-disk.

## The experiment on Pythia

The authors work with Pythia-70M and Pythia-160M, the sizes at which a clean induction head emerges mid-training with a sharp phase transition — the setting Nanda et al. (2024) dissected mechanistically. They choose one such head, define $f$ as its head-matching score on a probe set, and compute the EK-FAC influence of every training sequence in the specific slice of The Pile Pythia saw before the head formed. They then:

1. Remove the top-$k$ ranked samples (for a small fraction of the training batch) and resume training from a pre-formation checkpoint. The induction head's emergence is delayed, and in extreme ablations suppressed.
2. Inject additional samples drawn from the same distribution as the top-ranked ones. The head forms *earlier* in training.
3. Replicate both runs with random samples at matched volume. Nothing moves.

Downstream in-context learning performance tracks the interventions in the same direction: delaying head formation delays ICL, accelerating head formation accelerates ICL. That is the first direct causal evidence tying a specific set of training samples to an ICL-related capability through a specific interpretable circuit. The paper also reports a data-augmentation protocol that targets induction-head formation, with head-score gains it quotes in the +9% to +16% range on the two Pythia sizes; take the exact figures as the paper's claim rather than mine.

## Why LaTeX

Here is the finding that is harder to shrug off. When one inspects the top-ranked training samples, they are overwhelmingly LaTeX source, HTML, and XML. The explanation is almost mechanical. An induction head implements the algorithm $A B \dots A \to B$: find the previous occurrence of the current token, and copy the token that followed it last time. Structured markup is *exactly* that pattern realised across whole corpora. `\begin{equation}` is followed by `\end{equation}` with high probability; `<tag>` is followed by `</tag>`; and across a long document the opening tag reliably appears before the closing one. The sample's gradient, in parameter space, points down the direction that minimises its loss, and the direction that minimises its loss is also the direction that makes the model attend from closing tag back to opening tag — which is the direction that strengthens the induction head.

The claim is subtler than "LaTeX is good training data". It is that the induction head's *functional form* is maximally represented in a particular corner of the data, and the circuit forms earliest where its functional form appears. This frames induction-head emergence as a question about the alignment between the loss gradient and the circuit's parameter subspace, not about data cleanliness, and it suggests a general tool: for any circuit whose algorithm you can write down, the training samples that catalyse its formation are those whose loss gradient happens to point along the parameter directions the circuit occupies.

## A concrete anchor

The sketch below is the shape of a mechanistic-influence computation, not working code. In practice one uses the Bergson or similar library for the EK-FAC and gradient-store plumbing, and the per-sample gradients cost one backward pass each.

```python
import torch

def head_matching_score(model, probe_batch, layer, head):
    # probe_batch: sequences of form A B ... A, with target position = last A
    # We want attention from the last A to the previous B.
    out = model(probe_batch, return_attn=True)
    attn = out.attn[layer][:, head]          # (B, seq, seq)
    tgt = probe_batch["prev_B_position"]     # (B,) index of the previous B
    last = probe_batch["last_A_position"]    # (B,)
    return attn[torch.arange(len(tgt)), last, tgt].mean()

# Gradient of a mechanistic scalar w.r.t. all model params:
f_grad = torch.autograd.grad(
    head_matching_score(model, probe, L, h),
    model.parameters(),
)

# For each candidate training sample, compute grad of its loss once.
# Then apply the EK-FAC approximation of H^{-1}:
#   influence_j = -(f_grad)^T . H^{-1} . grad_j
# Rank samples by influence; the top is the pedigree of this head.
```

Note what has changed from the classical influence setup: the test functional is not a loss on a test example, it is a scalar that measures how much a specific attention head behaves like an induction head on a probe set. Everything downstream — the gradient, the Hessian-inverse, the ranking — is the same.

## What this implies in practice

For interpretability researchers, data attribution is now a tool you can point at any interpretable unit, not just at predictions. Found a mysterious SAE feature? Ask what training samples support its activation. The method lifts "where does this come from" from folklore to a numeric answer with a causal retraining backstop. For data curation, structured markup is doing more training work per token than its share of the corpus would suggest; the common practice of filtering it aggressively as low-value boilerplate is, at the margin, removing exactly the samples that catalyse a known capability. For scaling claims, when a new architecture or data mixture shifts the timing of in-context learning emergence, mechanistic attribution lets you check whether the shift happened at induction-head formation or somewhere else — and that distinction matters, because the two have different downstream consequences.

## Limits and open questions

The influence-function machinery is a first-order local approximation that assumes the leave-one-out counterfactual stays near $\hat\theta$. Multiple papers have shown the approximation breaks down for deep non-convex losses when retrained models move far from the original (Basu, Pope, Feizi 2021; Bae et al. 2022; K and Søgaard 2021). MDA's retraining experiments are precisely the empirical check that first-order rankings are, in this setting, tracking something real; but the general reliability of the first-order estimate at frontier scale is still contested, and nothing says a ranking that holds on Pythia-160M holds on a 70B-parameter model. Second, the paper demonstrates attribution on named circuits with pre-specified probe sets. Most of what a frontier LM does is not organised into cleanly named circuits, and the methodology inherits whatever selection effects the probe set carries: the ranking is for the unit you asked about, in the way you asked about it. Third, the LaTeX catalyst finding mixes a syntactic hypothesis (repetitive bracketing) with a semantic one (mathematical content); the paper's ablations narrow this gap but do not close it. Fourth, intervening on data to accelerate circuit formation is close enough to data poisoning that it should concern anyone using it: the same handle that speeds up induction heads could, in principle, be turned to install a very specific kind of circuit on purpose.

## Further reading

- Chen, Luo, Pan. *Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing the Training Origins of Interpretable LLM Units.* ICML 2026 oral. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21996>. The paper this post is about; the induction-head retraining experiment is in §4 and the LaTeX finding in §5.
- Olsson et al. *In-context Learning and Induction Heads.* Transformer Circuits, 2022. <https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/>. The original six-line case for induction heads as the carrier of ICL, with its own candid self-assessment of what the evidence does and does not support.
- Grosse, Bae, Anil, Elhage et al. *Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions.* arXiv:2308.03296, 2023. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03296>. The EK-FAC scaling that makes influence functions tractable at LM scale, with careful validation against PBRF.
- Park, Georgiev, Ilyas, Leclerc, Madry. *TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale.* ICML 2023. <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/park23c.html>. The sampling-based attribution alternative, with a different bias-variance trade-off than influence functions.
- Biderman et al. *Pythia: A Suite for Analyzing Large Language Models Across Training and Scaling.* ICML 2023. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01373>. Sixteen checkpointed models, public training data, reproducible data order. The only reason the MDA experiments can be run.
- Koh, Liang. *Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions.* ICML 2017. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04730>. The paper that put the implicit-function derivation of $I_j$ on the ML map; still the clearest exposition.
- Bae, Ng, Lo, Ghassemi, Grosse. *If Influence Functions Are the Answer, Then What Is the Question?* NeurIPS 2022. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05364>. The counter-case: when and why the first-order approximation fails in deep learning.
- Nanda, Rajamanoharan, Bloom, et al. *What Needs to Go Right for an Induction Head?* arXiv:2404.07129, 2024. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07129>. The mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits that pins down exactly when and how induction heads form during training.
